It fetches authentic SPHEREx infrared data (102 band photometry and FITS cutouts) from NASA’s IRSA service, while also providing locally cached FITS files for rapid offline access. The atlas visualizes stars and constellations using pre‑bundled public catalogues, and the lab lets users retrieve and inspect raw observations. Spectral and blink tools enable detailed multi‑epoch analysis, and the anomaly engine automatically flags data‑quality issues. By delivering real NASA data with fast, client‑side rendering and a unified UI, the project turns complex infrared datasets into an intuitive, research‑grade tool for education, citizen science, and professional analysis

What it does / How it works
COSMIC COMMONS is a single‑page web application that lets users explore the infrared universe in real time.

  • 3‑D Sky Atlas renders stars, constellations and target positions using pre‑bundled Hipparcos/Tycho data and IAU boundary files.
  • Research Lab queries NASA’s IRSA Simple Image Access (SIA) service for SPHEREx FITS cutouts, parses the first image HDU, and displays it instantly.
  • Spectral Explorer pulls the 102‑band SPHEREx photometric cube for any target, plots the full spectrum, and falls back to a locally cached archive for offline speed.
  • Blink Comparator fetches two epochs of the same target (different MJDs) and animates them to highlight motion or variability.
  • Anomaly Engine runs automated analyses on the full FITS set (local or remote) to flag data‑quality issues (outliers, noise spikes, missing frames).

All components share a common state manager (AppState) so selections (target, band, epoch) are instantly reflected across the UI.

Benefits

  • Instant access to authentic NASA SPHEREx data without requiring a separate data‑download step.
  • Zero‑install, shareable URL (deployed on Vercel) that works on any modern browser.
  • Fast offline fallback via a pre‑generated local FITS archive (200 files covering 10 curated high‑value targets).
  • Educational & research‑grade tool: users can visualize proper‑motion stars, compare epochs, and explore full infrared spectra.

Intended impact

  • Lower the barrier for students, citizen scientists, and professional astronomers to work with high‑quality infrared datasets.
  • Demonstrate how a modern web stack can serve large scientific archives (multi‑GB FITS) with sub‑second latency.
  • Provide a reusable codebase that other missions or surveys can fork to expose their own data through a browser‑first interface.

  • Build & deployment: Vercel (serverless functions, automatic CDN caching).
  • Data generation: Custom Node scripts (generateLocalArchive.cjs) that download SPHEREx FITS via IRSA and store them under public/data/local_archive.
  • Development environment: Windows 10, PowerShell, npm 8, VS Code.

Creativity

  • Integrated a full scientific workflow (catalog browsing → raw cutout → spectral analysis → temporal comparison → quality anomaly detection) into one cohesive UI.
  • Combined live NASA archive queries with a pre‑cached local archive to achieve both authenticity and speed.
  • Used WebGL‑light canvas rendering for high‑performance image display and custom image‑stretch algorithms for visual clarity.

Design considerations

  • Performance: minimized server latency by caching FITS locally and streaming only needed slices.
  • Scalability: modular API layer (observations / cutout) can be extended to other missions (e.g., JWST, HST) without rewiring the UI.
  • Usability: unified AppState context ensures selections propagate instantly; responsive design works on desktop and tablets.
  • Reliability: fallback to the local archive if IRSA is unreachable; build includes Vercel deployment protection to ensure continuous availability.
